overview.summary: Learn to turn raw business data into decisions with spreadsheets, SQL, Python, dashboards and AI assistants, and to check what the AI produces. Ten practical modules set in Indian businesses, a final assessment, and a portfolio project with a mentor.
overview.audience: students and graduates who want an entry-level data analyst role, or to use data well in any job
outcomes: Turn a vague business question into an analysis plan with a clear decision
Clean, combine and summarise data in Excel, SQL and Python (pandas)
Build a dashboard that tracks what matters and flags problems early
Use AI assistants to work faster, and verify everything they produce
Present a recommendation a manager can act on, backed by a portfolio project

skills.name: Data Literacy & Analytical Thinking
skills.description: Framing questions, knowing data types, and reading numbers critically.

skills.name: Data Cleaning & Preparation
skills.description: Finding and fixing duplicates, blanks, bad types and inconsistent values, with a record of every step.

skills.name: SQL & Database Analytics
skills.description: Querying databases: filtering, grouping, joining tables and window functions.

skills.name: Python for Data Analytics
skills.description: Loading, cleaning, summarising and joining data with pandas in a notebook.

skills.name: Spreadsheet Analysis with Excel
skills.description: Tables, lookups, PivotTables and formulas that answer business questions.

skills.name: Statistics for Decisions
skills.description: Spread, samples, bias and simple experiments: telling a real change from noise.

skills.name: Data Visualisation & Dashboards
skills.description: Choosing the right chart and building dashboards around decisions, in Power BI or Excel.

skills.name: AI-Assisted Analysis
skills.description: Using AI assistants and Copilot to speed up analysis, checking their output, and protecting personal data.

skills.name: Data Storytelling & Business Communication
skills.description: Turning analysis into a clear recommendation, with honest limits.

items.statement: Before I answer a question with numbers, I check exactly what is being asked.
I notice when a statistic in the news or on social media doesn’t add up.
I take the numbers in reports at face value.
I use formulas instead of working things out by hand.
I can summarise a long list in a spreadsheet quickly.
Spreadsheets with more than a few hundred rows overwhelm me.
I spot typos, duplicates and inconsistent entries in lists.
I keep a copy of the original file before I change any data.
I start working with data without checking it first.
I enjoy breaking a question into small, logical steps.
I’m comfortable learning an exact syntax step by step, like spreadsheet formulas.
Writing even simple code feels out of reach for me.
I ask how many people a survey asked before I trust its result.
I know an average can hide very different situations.
When two things happen together, I assume one causes the other.
I like automating tasks I have to repeat.
When a tool shows an error, I read it and try to fix it myself.
I avoid tasks that involve typing commands or code.
I choose charts that make the main point obvious.
I notice when a chart’s design exaggerates a difference.
I add as many charts as I can to show I’ve been thorough.
I use AI tools to speed up my studies or work.
I check an AI tool’s answer against another source before relying on it.
If an AI tool sounds confident, I trust its answer.
I can explain a complicated finding in two or three sentences.
I start a presentation with my main point.
I find it hard to say what my analysis means for a decision.

modules.title: Thinking like an analyst
modules.summary: Turn vague questions into answerable ones, know your data types, and read averages critically.
modules.outcome: Turn a vague business question into one you can answer with data.

learn.title: Start with the decision, not the data
learn.body: An analysis is only useful if it changes a decision. Before you open a spreadsheet, write down who will decide, what they will decide, and what would change their mind. “How are sales doing?” becomes “Should we keep the Diwali discount running in Pune next week?”: a question with an owner, a deadline and an action.

learn.title: Know your data types
learn.body: Some numbers can be added (revenue in ₹, minutes, quantities). Some only look like numbers (PIN codes, phone numbers, order IDs). Then there are categories (city, payment method), dates, and free text. Many early mistakes come from treating one type as another: averaging PIN codes, or sorting dates stored as text.

learn.title: Averages hide, distributions tell
learn.body: An average order value of ₹850 can mean every order is about ₹850, or that most orders are ₹300 and a few bulk orders are ₹20,000. Before you trust a single number, look at the spread: the minimum, the maximum and the median (the middle value).

tasks.title: Sharpen a vague question
tasks.prompt: A café chain’s owner asks: “Why are we losing customers?” Rewrite this as two or three specific questions you could answer with data. For each, say what data you would need and what decision it would inform.
tasks.hint: Name the time period, which customers you mean, and what “losing” looks like in the data (for example, no visit in 60 days).

tasks.title: Spot the wrong type
tasks.prompt: List five columns you would expect in an online store’s orders file. For each, give its data type and one mistake someone could make if they treated it as a different type.
tasks.hint: An order ID looks like a number. Would you ever add order IDs together?

reflection.prompt: Think of a decision you made recently: a phone, a course, a trip. What data did you use, and what data do you wish you had?
reflection.hint: Small personal decisions use the same habits as business ones.

quiz.title: The report by Friday

context.background: The founder says weekly orders “feel slower” and wants a report by Friday.
context.objective: Make the request answerable and useful.
context.information: 18 months of orders with date, city, basket value and customer ID.

quiz.question: What is the best first step?
options: Build a dashboard of every metric the order data lets you calculate, then look for what changed
Compare this week’s orders with last week’s, city by city, and send the founder the result
Agree with the founder which decision the report is for and how “slower” will be measured
Ask the tech team for every table they have, so nothing is missing when you start
quiz.explanation: Agreeing on the decision and the measure (for example, orders per week for the last 8 weeks against the same weeks last year) makes the work answerable and useful.
quiz.why_wrong: A dashboard of everything answers nothing in particular; one week against the last is noisy (festivals, salary days); asking for more data delays the work without knowing what is needed.
quiz.learning_outcome: Frame the question before touching the data.

quiz.title: The delivery app’s customer table
quiz.question: Which of these columns should never be averaged?
options: Customer PIN code
Delivery time in minutes
Order value in ₹
Items per order
quiz.explanation: A PIN code is a label written in digits. Its average is a meaningless number.
quiz.why_wrong: Delivery time, order value and items per order are real quantities, where an average (or a median) means something.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check a column’s type before you summarise it.

quiz.title: Fees at a study centre
quiz.scenario: A study centre records monthly fees for 50 students. 47 pay between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500; three corporate-sponsored students pay ₹30,000 each.
quiz.question: Which single number best describes what a typical student pays?
options: The mean (average) fee
The highest fee
The total fees divided by 12
The median fee
quiz.explanation: The three large fees pull the mean far above what most students pay (to about ₹4,000). The median stays around what the middle student pays, roughly ₹2,200–2,500.
quiz.why_wrong: The mean is distorted by the three outliers; the highest fee describes the exception; dividing by 12 confuses monthly and yearly figures.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use the median when a few extreme values distort the mean.

quiz.title: Dark mode and test scores
quiz.scenario: A coaching app finds that students who switch on dark mode score 12% higher in its tests. The product manager wants to make dark mode the default to raise scores.
quiz.question: What is the soundest response?
options: Agree, because a 12% difference across thousands of students is far too large to be a coincidence
Say dark-mode users may differ in other ways (more engaged, studying late), so test it first
Reject it, because a 12% rise is too small to justify changing the app’s default
Ask for light-mode users’ scores too, since the comparison needs both groups
quiz.explanation: Correlation is not causation: keen, heavy users may simply be the ones who pick dark mode. A randomised test, where some new users get dark mode by default, shows whether the setting itself changes scores.
quiz.why_wrong: A large gap can still come from who chooses dark mode rather than the setting itself; 12% would matter if it were real; light-mode scores are already in the comparison, and more of them can’t show cause.
quiz.learning_outcome: Two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

modules.title: Spreadsheets that answer questions
modules.summary: Tables, XLOOKUP and PivotTables: answer business questions in Excel or Google Sheets.
modules.outcome: Use tables, lookups and PivotTables to answer a business question in a spreadsheet.

learn.title: Make it a table first
learn.body: Format your data as a table (Ctrl+T in Excel): one header row, one row per record, no blank rows and no merged cells. A table grows with new data, so formulas, filters and PivotTables keep working, and you can refer to columns by name, like Orders[Value].

learn.title: Look things up with XLOOKUP
learn.body: XLOOKUP finds a value in one column and returns the matching value from another, such as a product’s category from a price list. Unlike VLOOKUP it can look left, matches exactly by default, and lets you say what to show when nothing is found: =XLOOKUP(A2, Products[SKU], Products[Category], "Not found").

learn.title: Summarise with a PivotTable
learn.body: A PivotTable groups and totals thousands of rows in seconds: revenue by city by month, or orders by payment method. Drag fields into Rows, Columns and Values, then switch Values between Sum, Count and Average as the question needs.

tasks.title: Plan a PivotTable
tasks.prompt: An online saree store’s orders table has: order date, city, category, payment method (UPI, card, cash on delivery), order value and returned (yes or no). Describe the PivotTable you would build to find which payment method has the highest return rate: what goes in Rows, what goes in Values, and how you calculate the rate.
tasks.hint: A return rate needs two numbers: returned orders and all orders.

tasks.title: Write the lookup
tasks.prompt: You have an orders sheet with SKU codes, and a separate price list with SKU, product name and category. Write the formula that brings the category into the orders sheet, and explain what happens when a SKU is missing from the price list.
tasks.hint: Look at XLOOKUP’s fourth argument.

reflection.prompt: What is one spreadsheet task you do, or have seen done, by hand that a table, a lookup or a PivotTable could do in seconds?
reflection.hint: Copying totals from one sheet to another counts.

quiz.question: Why turn a range of data into an Excel Table before analysing it?
options: It compresses the data, so large files open and recalculate noticeably faster
It checks new rows and removes duplicate records automatically as you type
Formulas and PivotTables pick up new rows, and columns can be used by name
It protects the range, so values can’t be changed without unlocking the sheet
quiz.explanation: Tables expand as rows are added and give columns names, so everything built on them stays correct as the data grows.
quiz.why_wrong: A table doesn’t shrink the file, remove duplicates or lock the data.
quiz.learning_outcome: Structure data as a table before analysing it.

quiz.title: Invoices and a product master
quiz.scenario: A distributor in Indore is matching 4,000 invoice lines to a 900-row product master. Some SKUs on the invoices are new and not yet in the master.
quiz.question: Which formula returns the product category, and shows “New SKU” when there is no match?
options: =XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU")
=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(B2, Master, 2, TRUE), "New SKU")
=XLOOKUP(Master[SKU], B2, Master[Category], "New SKU")
=IFNA(SUMIF(Master[SKU], B2, Master[Category]), "New SKU")
quiz.explanation: XLOOKUP takes the value to find, where to find it, what to return, and what to show if it isn’t found.
quiz.why_wrong: VLOOKUP with TRUE does an approximate match, so it can quietly return the wrong category instead of “New SKU”; the third option has the first two arguments swapped; SUMIF adds numbers and can’t return a text category.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use an exact-match lookup with a clear “not found” value.

quiz.title: Return rate by payment method
quiz.scenario: Your orders sheet has a Returned column with 1 for a returned order and 0 for a kept one. Payment method is in the Rows of your PivotTable.
quiz.question: Which Values setting shows the return rate for each payment method directly?
options: Sum of Returned, shown as % of Column Total
Count of Returned
Max of Returned
Average of Returned
quiz.explanation: The average of a column of 1s and 0s is the share of 1s: the return rate.
quiz.why_wrong: Sum counts the returns, and as % of Column Total it shows each method’s share of all returns, not its own rate; Count counts every order; Max is 1 as soon as one order is returned.
quiz.learning_outcome: Averaging a 1/0 column gives a rate.

quiz.title: GST on every row
quiz.scenario: Cell F1 holds the GST rate. In C2 you write =B2*$F$1 and fill it down to C500.
quiz.question: What do the dollar signs in $F$1 do?
options: Tell Excel to treat F1 as currency, so every result shows in rupees
Keep the reference fixed on F1 in every row, while B2 becomes B3, B4…
Make F1 a named constant that nobody else can edit
Round each row’s result to two decimal places, as GST requires
quiz.explanation: The dollar signs make an absolute reference: it doesn’t change when the formula is copied.
quiz.why_wrong: Dollar signs don’t format currency, lock cells or round anything.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use absolute references for values every row should share.

modules.title: Cleaning messy data
modules.summary: Profile data, fix duplicates, dates and inconsistent categories, and handle blanks honestly.
modules.outcome: Find and fix the problems that make analysis wrong, and keep a record of each fix.

learn.title: Profile before you clean
learn.body: Count the rows, then check every column: how many blanks, how many unique values, the minimum and maximum. Profiling shows what is broken: “Bengaluru”, “Bangalore” and “BLR” in one city column, ages of 0 and 212, dates in two formats.

learn.title: Fix the cause, and keep a record
learn.body: Standardise categories with a mapping table, trim spaces, convert text into proper dates and numbers, and remove true duplicates, such as the same order ID twice. Never do it silently: keep the raw file untouched and write down each step so anyone can repeat it. Power Query in Excel, or a Python script, makes the steps repeatable.

learn.title: Missing is not zero
learn.body: A blank delivery time is unknown, not 0 minutes. Decide column by column: leave it blank and exclude it, fill it from another source, or flag it. Say how many rows each choice affects, and ask whether the missing rows are different from the rest.

tasks.title: Write a cleaning plan
tasks.prompt: A hospital chain’s appointment export has: patient ID, appointment date (some as 03/04/2026, some as 2026-04-03), department (“Cardio”, “cardiology”, “CARDIOLOGY ”), doctor, fee (some “₹500”, some “500”) and status. Write a step-by-step cleaning plan: what you would check and fix in each column.
tasks.hint: Is 03/04/2026 the 3rd of April or the 4th of March? How could you find out?

tasks.title: Decide about blanks
tasks.prompt: In a delivery dataset, 6% of rows have no delivery time. Give two ways to handle them, and explain how each choice could change the average delivery time you report.
tasks.hint: Who is likely to be missing: fast deliveries, slow ones, or a random mix?

reflection.prompt: What is the messiest data you have seen: a form, a contact list, an attendance register? What would you fix first, and why?
reflection.hint: Think about which problem would cause the biggest wrong answer.

quiz.title: Bookings and payments
quiz.scenario: An event-ticketing startup’s bookings export has 5,200 rows, but the payments team counts 5,000 payments. 200 booking IDs appear twice, and each pair is identical in every column.
quiz.question: What is the right action?
options: Delete all 400 rows that share a booking ID, since you can’t tell which copy is real
Keep every row, because removing data could hide bookings the payments team missed
Remove the 200 exact duplicates, keeping one copy of each, and note it in the cleaning log
Merge each pair by averaging their values, so nothing from either row is lost
quiz.explanation: Identical rows with the same ID are true duplicates: keep one of each and record the change so the numbers can be reconciled.
quiz.why_wrong: Deleting both copies loses 200 real bookings; keeping them double-counts; averaging identical rows changes nothing and hides the problem.
quiz.learning_outcome: Remove true duplicates, keep one copy, and log it.

quiz.question: An export’s dates look like 04/05/2026, 13/05/2026 and 28/02/2026. What format are they in?
options: Day/month/year
Month/day/year
Year/month/day
It can’t be worked out
quiz.explanation: Values like 13 and 28 in the first position can’t be months, so the first number is the day.
quiz.why_wrong: Month/day/year would have no first number above 12; year/month/day would start with the year; the large first values settle it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use impossible values to work out an ambiguous date format.

quiz.question: A city column contains “Bengaluru”, “Bangalore”, “bangalore ” and “BLR”. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Delete the rows that don’t say “Bengaluru”, since they were entered incorrectly
Leave them as they are, because a PivotTable groups similar spellings together
Use Find and Replace on “Bangalore”, the most common variant, and leave the rest as they are
Trim spaces, map every variant to one name in a lookup table, then check nothing is left
quiz.explanation: A mapping table handles every variant the same way, is easy to extend, and the final check catches anything new.
quiz.why_wrong: Deleting rows loses real data; a PivotTable treats each spelling as a different city; one Find and Replace misses the other variants and the trailing space.
quiz.learning_outcome: Standardise categories with a mapping, then verify.

quiz.title: The missing delivery times
quiz.scenario: In a food-delivery dataset, 8% of orders have no delivery time. Most of them are orders the customer cancelled after a long wait.
quiz.question: If you drop those rows and report the average delivery time, what happens?
options: Nothing changes, because rows with no delivery time are simply left out of every average
The average looks better than reality, because the slowest cases are the ones left out
The average looks longer than reality, because the cancelled orders were the slowest
The average can’t be trusted at all, so no delivery figure should be reported
quiz.explanation: The missing rows aren’t random: they are mostly the slowest orders. Dropping them makes delivery look faster than it is.
quiz.why_wrong: Missing rows matter when they differ from the rest; leaving out the slowest orders makes the average shorter, not longer; the average can still be reported, as long as you say what it leaves out.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask why data is missing before you drop it.

modules.title: SQL foundations: asking a database questions
modules.summary: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING: filter, group and summarise data in a database.
modules.outcome: Write SELECT queries that filter, sort, group and summarise data.

learn.title: One question, one query
learn.body:
SQL reads almost like a sentence: SELECT the columns, FROM a table, WHERE rows match a condition, ORDER BY a column.

SELECT city, order_value
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY order_value DESC;

learn.title: GROUP BY turns rows into answers
learn.body:
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise rows, and GROUP BY decides the groups.

SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(order_value) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;

Every column in SELECT is either in the GROUP BY or inside a summary function.

learn.title: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
learn.body: WHERE works before grouping (only paid orders); HAVING works after (only cities with more than 100 orders). A query runs in this order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. Knowing the order explains most “why won’t this work?” moments.

tasks.title: Write the query
tasks.prompt: A table payments(payment_id, user_id, method, amount, paid_at) holds a fintech app’s transactions. Write a query that shows, for each payment method, the number of payments and the total amount in April 2026, largest total first.
tasks.hint: Filter the dates in WHERE, then GROUP BY method.

tasks.title: Explain a query in plain words
tasks.prompt:
Explain what this query returns, as you would to a manager who doesn’t know SQL:
SELECT city, AVG(delivery_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM deliveries WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 ORDER BY avg_minutes;
tasks.hint: Why might the HAVING line be there?

reflection.prompt: Which questions at a business you know could be answered with a single GROUP BY query? Write two.
reflection.hint: Think “for each …, how many / how much …?”

quiz.question: Which query counts the orders in each city?
options: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM orders;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders ORDER BY city;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, SUM(order_id) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY city makes one group per city, and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each.
quiz.why_wrong: COUNT(DISTINCT city) counts how many cities there are; mixing city and COUNT(*) without GROUP BY is an error in most databases, and ORDER BY only sorts; adding up order IDs means nothing.
quiz.learning_outcome: GROUP BY plus a summary function answers “for each …”.

quiz.question: You want cities whose total revenue is above ₹10 lakh. Which clause filters on that total?
options: HAVING SUM(order_value) > 1000000
WHERE SUM(order_value) > 1000000
ORDER BY SUM(order_value) > 1000000
GROUP BY SUM(order_value) > 1000000
quiz.explanation: Totals exist only after grouping, so they are filtered with HAVING.
quiz.why_wrong: WHERE runs before grouping and can’t use SUM; ORDER BY sorts, it doesn’t filter; you can’t group by a condition on a total.
quiz.learning_outcome: Filter groups with HAVING, rows with WHERE.

quiz.title: Leads without a phone number
quiz.scenario: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leads WHERE phone = NULL; returns 0, though many leads have no phone number.
quiz.question: Why?
options: The table has no leads with a missing phone number, so 0 is right
COUNT(*) skips rows where any of the columns is NULL
NULL needs quotes, as in WHERE phone = 'NULL'
“= NULL” is never true; it should be WHERE phone IS NULL
quiz.explanation: NULL means unknown, so “phone = NULL” is never true. SQL uses IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.
quiz.why_wrong: The leads do have missing phones; COUNT(*) counts rows whatever their values; 'NULL' in quotes is just the text NULL.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test for missing values with IS NULL.

quiz.title: Ratings with gaps
quiz.scenario: A table ratings(order_id, stars) has 1,000 orders. 400 have no rating (NULL). AVG(stars) returns 4.2.
quiz.question: What does 4.2 describe?
options: The average across all 1,000 orders, counting missing ratings as 0
The average of the 600 rated orders; AVG ignores NULLs
The median rating
Nothing: the NULLs cause an error
quiz.explanation: Summary functions skip NULLs, so 4.2 is the average among the 60% who rated. A report should say so: “4.2 stars among the 60% of orders that were rated.”
quiz.why_wrong: Missing ratings aren’t treated as 0; AVG is a mean, not a median; NULLs don’t cause an error.
quiz.learning_outcome: Know who is in an average before you report it.

modules.title: SQL for real questions: joins and windows
modules.summary: Combine tables with joins, avoid double counting, and compare rows with window functions.
modules.outcome: Combine tables with joins and compare rows with window functions.

learn.title: Joins connect facts to context
learn.body: An orders table knows each customer_id; a customers table knows their city and sign-up date. An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and leaves blanks where nothing matches: the way to find customers who never ordered.

learn.title: Watch the row count
learn.body: A join can multiply rows. If one customer has three saved addresses and you join orders to addresses, each order appears three times and revenue triples. Count the rows, and check a total, before and after every join.

learn.title: Window functions compare without collapsing
learn.body:
GROUP BY squashes rows into groups; a window function keeps every row and adds context: a running total, a rank within a city, last month’s value.

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at) gives each user a running total.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at) = 1 marks their first payment.

tasks.title: Find the silent customers
tasks.prompt: Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, signed_up) and orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value). Write a query that lists customers who signed up in 2026 but have never ordered.
tasks.hint: LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows where the order side is empty.

tasks.title: First order or repeat?
tasks.prompt: Using the orders table, describe (or write) how you would mark each order as a customer’s first order or a repeat order, then work out what share of April 2026 revenue came from repeat orders.
tasks.hint: ROW_NUMBER over each customer’s orders, by date.

reflection.prompt: Have you ever seen a number that was “too good to be true”? Could a join that duplicated rows have explained it?
reflection.hint: Doubled revenue is a classic sign.

quiz.question: Which query lists customers who have no orders?
options: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_id IS NULL;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NOT NULL;
quiz.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and those with no orders have NULL on the order side.
quiz.why_wrong: An INNER JOIN drops customers without orders, so the filter finds nothing; the orders table alone can’t show customers who never ordered; IS NOT NULL keeps the customers who did order.
quiz.learning_outcome: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL finds what’s missing.

quiz.title: Revenue that grew overnight
quiz.scenario: An analyst joins orders (10,000 rows, ₹82 lakh revenue) to customer_addresses, where some customers have two or three saved addresses. The joined table shows ₹1.3 crore.
quiz.question: What most likely happened?
options: Orders were repeated once for each matching address, inflating the total
The join added orders for addresses that had no customer linked to them
Revenue was stored in rupees in one table and in paise in the other
Orders placed after the first query ran were included in the second
quiz.explanation: A one-to-many join repeats each order for every address its customer has, so summing order values double or triple counts.
quiz.why_wrong: A join can’t create orders that weren’t in the orders table; a unit mix-up would change every row by the same factor, not only some; the data didn’t change between the two queries.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check totals after a join to catch double counting.

quiz.question: Which expression numbers each customer’s orders 1, 2, 3… from the first?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, order_date)
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_date ORDER BY customer_id)
SUM(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
quiz.explanation: PARTITION BY restarts the numbering for each customer, and ORDER BY order_date puts the first order first.
quiz.why_wrong: Without PARTITION BY customer_id the numbering never restarts for each customer; RANK partitioned by date ranks customers within each day; a running sum of order IDs isn’t a count.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use ROW_NUMBER to find firsts and sequences.

quiz.question: You need every order shown next to its city’s average order value, to flag unusually large orders. Which approach keeps every order row?
options: GROUP BY city, then compare each order with the averages by eye
AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) alongside each order
SELECT DISTINCT city, AVG(value), sorted by the average
HAVING AVG(value) > value after a GROUP BY on city
quiz.explanation: A window average adds the city’s average to every order row without collapsing the rows.
quiz.why_wrong: Reading averages by eye doesn’t put them on the order rows; DISTINCT with AVG returns one row per city; HAVING filters groups and can’t compare each order with its group.
quiz.learning_outcome: Window functions add group context without losing detail.

modules.title: Statistics that change decisions
modules.summary: Variation, samples, bias and A/B tests: tell a real change from noise.
modules.outcome: Use spread, samples and simple experiments to tell a real change from noise.

learn.title: Variation is normal
learn.body: Daily orders bounce around even when nothing has changed: weekends, salary days, rain, festivals. Before celebrating a jump, compare it with how much the number usually moves, for example the range or the standard deviation over recent weeks. A change inside the usual range is probably noise.

learn.title: Samples, margins and who answered
learn.body: A survey of 200 students isn’t every student. The smaller the sample, the wider the range around the result: “72% are satisfied” from 50 answers could easily be 60% or 85% for everyone, while from 2,000 answers it is within a couple of points. Ask who answered too: happy or angry customers reply more than everyone else.

learn.title: A/B tests answer “did it work?”
learn.body: Split users at random: half see the old checkout, half the new one, at the same time. Random assignment balances everything else, so a clear difference can be credited to the change. Decide the measure and how long the test runs before you start: stopping the moment it “looks good” fools you.

tasks.title: Design a test
tasks.prompt: An edtech app wants to know whether a ₹99 first-month offer brings more paid sign-ups than a 7-day free trial. Design an A/B test: who is in it, how they are split, what you measure, how long it runs, and what result would make you pick a winner.
tasks.hint: What could go wrong if the offer ran only in one city, or only in the first week?

tasks.title: Noise or signal?
tasks.prompt: A shop’s daily sales were between ₹38,000 and ₹52,000 for the last 60 days. Yesterday, after a new shelf layout, sales were ₹54,000. Write what you would tell the owner, and what you would check before concluding that the layout worked.
tasks.hint: One day against a pattern.

reflection.prompt: When have you seen a survey or “study” quoted that you now doubt? What would you want to know about how it was done?
reflection.hint: How many people, who were they, and who chose them?

quiz.question: In an A/B test, why are users assigned to the two groups at random?
options: So the test finishes sooner, because users don’t have to be sorted into groups
So both groups end up with exactly the same number of users every day
So the groups are alike except for the change, and a difference can be credited to it
So users can’t choose a version, which would break the app’s terms of use
quiz.explanation: Randomisation spreads every other difference (age, city, device, habits) evenly between the groups.
quiz.why_wrong: Randomising doesn’t make a test faster, guarantee equal group sizes, or exist to stop users choosing.
quiz.learning_outcome: Random assignment is what makes a test fair.

quiz.title: Two app ratings
quiz.scenario: App A shows 4.9 stars from 40 reviews. App B shows 4.6 stars from 52,000 reviews.
quiz.question: Which statement is most defensible?
options: App B’s rating is the more reliable estimate; App A’s could change a lot with more reviews
App A is clearly better, because its rating is higher and recent reviews matter more
Both are equally reliable, because a star rating is an average either way
They can’t be compared at all, because the apps have different numbers of reviews
quiz.explanation: With 40 reviews a few new ones can move the average a lot; 52,000 reviews pin it down closely.
quiz.why_wrong: A higher average from 40 reviews can’t show A is better; reliability depends on how many ratings sit behind each average; the different review counts are exactly what tells you which to trust more.
quiz.learning_outcome: Small samples give uncertain results.

quiz.title: The early winner
quiz.scenario: A team checks its A/B test every hour, and stops it on day 2 because the new design is ahead by 9%.
quiz.question: What is the main risk?
options: None: a 9% lead after two days of traffic is enough to be confident the new design is better
Two days is too short for the servers to show both designs to a large enough number of users
Checking every hour slows the website down and changes how users behave
Early leads swing by chance; stopping at the first good moment often crowns a false winner
quiz.explanation: Results swing a lot early on. Checking constantly and stopping when ahead almost guarantees you’ll catch a lucky moment.
quiz.why_wrong: A two-day lead can be pure chance; showing two designs isn’t limited to a certain number of days; checking results doesn’t change what users see.
quiz.learning_outcome: Fix a test’s length before it starts.

quiz.title: The satisfied members
quiz.scenario: A gym chain surveys members who have just renewed, and 90% say they are “very satisfied”. The CEO wants “90% of our members are very satisfied” in an advert.
quiz.question: What is the problem?
options: 90% is too high to believe; honest satisfaction surveys of gym members rarely go above 70%
Only members who renewed were asked; those who left are missing, so it overstates satisfaction
The survey needed more questions, about equipment and trainers, to measure satisfaction properly
Advertising rules allow survey results only when an outside agency ran the survey
quiz.explanation: Asking only people who stayed leaves out those who left: a selection bias that flatters the result.
quiz.why_wrong: A high number can be true for the group asked; more questions don’t fix who was asked; the problem is the sample, not who ran the survey.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check who was left out of a sample.

modules.title: Python and pandas for analysis
modules.summary: Load, clean, summarise and join data with pandas, and check each step.
modules.outcome: Load, clean, summarise and join data with pandas in a notebook.

learn.title: Why Python when there’s Excel?
learn.body: Python repeats your steps exactly on next month’s file, handles millions of rows, and records every step in a notebook anyone can rerun. pandas is its table library: a DataFrame is a sheet you can program. You can run it free in Google Colab, or inside Excel with Python in Excel.

learn.title: The everyday moves
learn.body:
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") loads a file.
df.info() and df.describe() profile it.
df[df["city"] == "Pune"] filters rows.
df.groupby("city")["value"].sum() summarises.
df.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left") joins tables.
pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], dayfirst=True) turns Indian-style dates into real dates.

learn.title: Check as you go
learn.body: After every step, look at the shape (df.shape), a few rows (df.head()) and a total you know. If revenue changes after a merge, rows were duplicated. Leave a short comment saying why each step exists: next month, you will be the person who needs it.

tasks.title: Plan the notebook
tasks.prompt: You receive a monthly CSV of 300,000 UPI transactions (txn_id, user_id, merchant_category, amount, txn_time, status). Write the pandas steps, as code or in plain words, to find the five merchant categories with the highest value of successful transactions in May 2026.
tasks.hint: Filter on status, turn txn_time into a date, then group.

tasks.title: Read the code
tasks.prompt:
Explain what this code does, line by line, and one thing that could go wrong:
df = pd.read_csv("leads.csv")
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="phone")
df["source"] = df["source"].str.strip().str.lower()
summary = df.groupby("source").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
tasks.hint: Are two leads with the same phone number always the same person?

reflection.prompt: What repetitive data task would you most like to automate? List the steps a script would follow.
reflection.hint: Anything you do every week in the same order is a candidate.

quiz.question: Which line gives the total order value for each city?
options: df.groupby("value")["city"].sum()
df["value"].sum() / df["city"].nunique()
df.groupby("city")["value"].sum()
df.pivot("city", "value").sum()
quiz.explanation: groupby makes one group per city; selecting "value" and summing gives each city’s total.
quiz.why_wrong: Grouping by value and summing city mixes up the two columns; total value divided by the number of cities is one average, not a total per city; pivot with these arguments doesn’t give city totals.
quiz.learning_outcome: groupby plus an aggregate summarises by category.

quiz.title: Indian dates in pandas
quiz.scenario: A column holds dates written the Indian way, such as "05/04/2026" for 5 April 2026.
quiz.question: Which line reads them correctly as dates?
options: pd.to_datetime(df["date"], dayfirst=True)
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")
df["date"].astype("datetime64[ns]")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
quiz.explanation: dayfirst=True tells pandas the first number is the day. Without it, pandas guesses the format and can read an ambiguous date like 05/04/2026 month-first, as 4 May.
quiz.why_wrong: errors="coerce" only blanks dates it can’t read, and astype also reads 05/04 month-first, so April and May still swap; the format %m/%d/%Y says the month comes first, the wrong way round.
quiz.learning_outcome: Tell pandas the date format; never let it guess.

quiz.question: orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left"): what happens to orders whose customer_id isn’t in customers?
options: They are dropped, because they have nothing to match in customers
The merge stops with an error naming the missing customer_ids
They are matched to the nearest customer_id that does exist
They are kept, with the customer columns empty (NaN)
quiz.explanation: A left merge keeps every row of the left table; unmatched rows get NaN in the right table’s columns.
quiz.why_wrong: Dropping unmatched rows is what an inner merge does; pandas doesn’t raise an error for unmatched keys; it never matches to a “nearest” key.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the merge type for the rows you must keep.

quiz.question: Which line keeps only successful transactions above ₹5,000?
options: df[df["status"] == "success" and df["amount"] > 5000]
df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]
df.filter("success", 5000)
df[(df["status"] == "success") | (df["amount"] > 5000)]
quiz.explanation: pandas combines conditions with & (and) and | (or), and each condition needs its own brackets.
quiz.why_wrong: Python’s “and” raises an error with whole columns; filter selects columns by name; | means “or”, which would keep failed transactions above ₹5,000 too.
quiz.learning_outcome: Combine pandas conditions with & and brackets.

modules.title: Dashboards people use
modules.summary: Choose the right chart, design dashboards around decisions, and check what Copilot drafts.
modules.outcome: Choose the right chart and build a dashboard around the decisions it supports.

learn.title: Pick the chart for the question
learn.body: Change over time: a line chart. Comparing categories: a bar chart, sorted. Part of a whole: a stacked bar, or a pie for two or three parts only. Relationship between two numbers: a scatter plot. When people need exact values, a well-formatted table is fine.

learn.title: A dashboard answers three questions
learn.body: Are we on track (the key number against its target)? Where is the problem (a breakdown by city, channel or product)? What changed (the trend against last period)? Put the most important number top left, keep each page to one purpose, and use colour only to draw attention to what needs action.

learn.title: Power BI in practice
learn.body: Power BI connects to Excel, databases and files, and builds an interactive report on a data model. Measures written in DAX, such as Revenue = SUM(Orders[Value]), are reused across visuals, and visual calculations add running totals or moving averages inside a chart. Copilot can draft measures and pages; always check its numbers against a total you trust before sharing.

tasks.title: Sketch the dashboard
tasks.prompt: The regional manager of a 40-store pharmacy chain wants a weekly dashboard. Describe one page: the 3–4 key numbers at the top, the charts below, the filters, and what decision each part helps them make.
tasks.hint: What would make them pick up the phone to a store manager?

tasks.title: Fix a bad chart
tasks.prompt: Describe a chart you have seen that was hard to read (a 3D pie, too many colours, an axis that doesn’t start at zero). Explain what was wrong, and how you would redraw it.
tasks.hint: Would a sorted bar chart say it more clearly?

reflection.prompt: Which number at your college, job or home would be worth tracking on a dashboard? What would you do differently if it went down?
reflection.hint: A good dashboard number leads to an action.

quiz.question: Which chart best shows monthly revenue over the last 18 months?
options: A pie chart
A scatter plot
A line chart
A donut chart
quiz.explanation: A line chart shows change over time and makes trends and seasonality easy to see.
quiz.why_wrong: Pie and donut charts show parts of a whole, not time; a scatter plot shows the relationship between two numbers.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use line charts for trends over time.

quiz.title: The giant jump
quiz.scenario: A bar chart shows this quarter’s sales at ₹102 lakh against ₹100 lakh last quarter, but the new bar looks five times taller.
quiz.question: What is most likely wrong?
options: The value axis starts near ₹99 lakh instead of zero, exaggerating a 2% rise
The data is wrong: a 2% rise can’t produce a bar that much taller
The bars are drawn in 3D, which makes the nearer bar look larger
The two quarters are measured in different units, so the bars can’t be compared directly
quiz.explanation: Bar lengths are read as sizes; starting the axis near the values makes a small difference look huge.
quiz.why_wrong: The numbers are fine; nothing suggests 3D or a units mix-up; the axis scale is what exaggerates the difference.
quiz.learning_outcome: Start bar chart axes at zero.

quiz.title: The 30-minute promise
quiz.scenario: The operations head of a food-delivery company wants to see at a glance whether any city is missing its 30-minute delivery target.
quiz.question: What should the top of the dashboard show?
options: A table of every late order, so the head can read through the details
The national average delivery time, compared with last month
Total orders per city, since the busiest cities are the likeliest to be late
Each city’s on-time delivery % against the target, below-target cities highlighted
quiz.explanation: The question is “which city is off target?”, so the top shows that measure for each city with problems highlighted.
quiz.why_wrong: Every late order is too much detail; one national average hides which city is off target; busy cities aren’t necessarily the late ones.
quiz.learning_outcome: Design a dashboard around the decision it supports.

quiz.title: Two repeat rates
quiz.scenario: Copilot in Power BI drafts a measure, Repeat Customer Rate, that returns 74%. Your earlier SQL analysis found 41% for the same period.
quiz.question: What should you do first?
options: Publish Copilot’s figure, as it uses the live data model rather than an older query
Read the DAX it wrote, compare its definition and period with yours, then reconcile
Report both numbers side by side and let readers decide which to trust
Rerun your SQL until it matches Copilot, since the dashboard is what people see
quiz.explanation: Two methods disagreeing usually means two definitions. Reading the generated DAX shows what it actually calculates, so you can fix whichever is wrong.
quiz.why_wrong: Using the live model doesn’t make a definition right; two unexplained numbers confuse readers; forcing your SQL to match hides which definition is correct.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reconcile AI-drafted measures against a trusted result.

modules.title: AI as your analysis partner
modules.summary: Prompt AI assistants well, check everything they produce, and keep personal data safe.
modules.outcome: Use AI assistants to speed up analysis, and check their work before anyone relies on it.

learn.title: What AI is good at
learn.body: Drafting SQL and pandas code from a plain-English question, explaining unfamiliar formulas, suggesting cleaning steps, summarising findings and proposing charts. Copilot in Excel and Power BI, and general assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, can all do this. They work best when you give them the table names, the columns and what each column means.

learn.title: Where it goes wrong
learn.body: AI can write code that runs but answers a different question, invent column names, mishandle dates or missing values, and state wrong numbers confidently. Treat its output like a new colleague’s first draft: read it, run it on a small sample you can check by hand, and compare totals with a source you trust.

learn.title: Protect people’s data
learn.body: Don’t paste personal data (names, phone numbers, Aadhaar numbers, health details) into public AI tools. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 allows personal data to be used only for a lawful purpose, with the person’s consent or for a few uses the Act permits, and it must be kept safe. Use the tools your organisation approves; otherwise share only column names and a few made-up rows, and run the resulting code on the real data yourself.

tasks.title: Write a good prompt
tasks.prompt: You need the share of repeat customers in each month, from tables orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value) and customers(customer_id, city, signed_up). Write the prompt you would give an AI assistant to draft the SQL, then list three checks you would run on what it returns.
tasks.hint: Define “repeat customer” in the prompt, or the assistant will choose a definition for you.

tasks.title: Catch the error
tasks.prompt: An AI assistant summarises a sales file: “Revenue grew 40% in Q2, driven by Chennai.” Describe how you would check both parts of that sentence before putting it in a report.
tasks.hint: Recalculate from the raw data, and check which dates it used for Q2.

reflection.prompt: Where would you trust an AI assistant fully, and where would you always check its work? Why the difference?
reflection.hint: Think about the cost of a mistake in each case.

quiz.question: Which prompt is most likely to get correct SQL from an AI assistant?
options: “Write a SQL query that finds repeat customers in my orders table for 2026, month by month. Make it efficient and easy to read.”
“You are an expert data analyst with 20 years of experience. Analyse my sales data thoroughly and tell me about repeat customers.”
“Table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value): for each 2026 month, what % of customers had ordered before? PostgreSQL.”
“Using my company database, calculate the repeat customer rate for every month of 2026 and show the results as a line chart.”
quiz.explanation: It names the table and columns, defines the measure precisely, sets the period and says which database, leaving little to guess.
quiz.why_wrong: They leave out the table and its columns, a precise definition of a repeat customer, or both, so the assistant has to guess.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give AI the schema, the definition and the goal.

quiz.title: Code that runs
quiz.scenario: AI-written pandas code runs without errors and reports an average order value of ₹1,240.
quiz.question: What is the best way to check it?
options: Work out the same figure another way for a month you know, such as with a PivotTable
Trust it: code that runs on the full file without errors has been checked by Python
Ask the assistant to double-check its own code and confirm the figure
Compare it with last year’s average order value; if it’s close, it’s right
quiz.explanation: An independent calculation is the only real check: code can run perfectly and still compute the wrong thing.
quiz.why_wrong: Running without errors says nothing about correctness; the assistant checking itself isn’t independent; last year’s figure can’t confirm this year’s calculation.
quiz.learning_outcome: Verify AI output with an independent calculation.

quiz.title: The patient list
quiz.scenario: You want an AI assistant’s help cleaning a list of 20,000 patients with names, phone numbers and diagnoses.
quiz.question: What is the right approach?
options: Paste the whole file into a free AI chatbot, since it deletes conversations once you close the window
Remove the diagnosis column first, then share the names and phone numbers, which aren’t sensitive
Email the file to a friend who is good with AI and ask them to clean it
Use an approved tool, or share only the column names and made-up rows and run the code yourself
quiz.explanation: Personal and health data must stay within approved systems. Sharing the structure with made-up rows gets the help without exposing anyone.
quiz.why_wrong: You can’t be sure a free chatbot doesn’t keep what you paste; names and phone numbers are personal data on their own; sending the file to a friend exposes it too.
quiz.learning_outcome: Never share personal data with unapproved AI tools.

quiz.title: The column that isn’t there
quiz.scenario: AI-written SQL refers to a column customers.lifetime_value, which doesn’t exist in your database.
quiz.question: What does this tell you?
options: The database is missing a column the query needs, so ask IT to add lifetime_value to the table
It guessed your schema: give it the real table definitions and re-check the whole query
Create the column and fill it with sample values so the query can run
Remove that line; if the rest of the query runs, its result can be trusted
quiz.explanation: An invented column shows the assistant was guessing, so other parts may be guesses too. Supply the schema and re-check everything.
quiz.why_wrong: lifetime_value was invented, not missing; filling it with made-up values corrupts the result; a query that runs can still be wrong.
quiz.learning_outcome: An invented detail means: re-check the whole answer.

modules.title: From numbers to decisions
modules.summary: Lead with the recommendation, turn findings into actions, and be honest about limits.
modules.outcome: Turn an analysis into a clear recommendation a manager can act on.

learn.title: Lead with the answer
learn.body: Start with the recommendation and the number behind it: “Move ₹2 lakh from Meta to Google Search in Pune: Search brings customers at ₹310 each against ₹780 on Meta.” Then the evidence, then the caveats. Most managers read the first two lines and decide whether to read on.

learn.title: So what, and now what?
learn.body: For every chart, say what it shows and what it means for the decision. “Returns are 18% for cash-on-delivery orders and 6% for UPI” is a finding. “Offering ₹30 off for paying by UPI could cut returns” is the insight, with an action.

learn.title: Be honest about uncertainty
learn.body: State the period, the data source, the sample size and what you couldn’t check. A recommendation with clear limits earns more trust than a confident one that later falls apart, and it tells the reader what to watch next.

tasks.title: Write the first paragraph
tasks.prompt: You found that a D2C skincare brand’s customers who start with the trial kit are 2.3 times more likely to buy again within 60 days than customers who start with a full-size product (14,000 customers, January–June 2026). Write the opening paragraph of a memo to the founder, with your recommendation.
tasks.hint: Recommendation first, evidence second, one honest caveat.

tasks.title: Turn findings into actions
tasks.prompt: Three findings from a college canteen’s sales data: 60% of sales happen between 12:30 and 1:30 pm; the queue takes 14 minutes at peak; 30% of students who arrive at peak leave without buying. Write one insight and one action for each finding.
tasks.hint: What could the canteen change by next week?

reflection.prompt: Think of a presentation or message that persuaded you. What did the person do that you could use in your own reports?
reflection.hint: Notice what came first, and what they left out.

quiz.question: Which opening line is best for an update to a busy manager?
options: “This report analyses 14 tables and 2.1 million rows from our order, return and payment systems.”
“Data was collected from several sources over six months and cleaned with a documented process.”
“Recommendation: pause cash on delivery in Tier-3 cities, where COD returns cost about ₹4 lakh a month.”
“Here are 25 charts covering sales, returns and payments, organised by region and by month.”
quiz.explanation: It leads with an action, the evidence and the cost, so the manager can decide straight away.
quiz.why_wrong: They describe the work done, not what was found or what to do.
quiz.learning_outcome: Lead with the recommendation and its impact.

quiz.question: Which is an insight with an action, rather than just a finding?
options: “40% of carts are abandoned at the delivery fee; showing it on the product page could help.”
“The average order value is ₹640, slightly higher than in the same month last year.”
“We now have 12,000 customers, most of them in Maharashtra and Karnataka, up from 9,000 last year.”
“Sales were higher in October, when the festive season began across the country.”
quiz.explanation: It links a specific problem to a cause and a change worth testing.
quiz.why_wrong: They are facts, even with context added; none says what to do about it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Turn findings into insights by adding “so what” and “now what”.

quiz.title: Festive data
quiz.scenario: Your analysis of a jewellery brand’s website rests on three weeks of data, all during Diwali.
quiz.question: What should your memo say about it?
options: Nothing: mentioning limits would make the reader doubt the whole analysis
That the results are certain, because the festive weeks have the most orders of the whole year
Remove the festive weeks, and say there isn’t yet enough normal-month data to report anything
That it covers only three festive weeks, which may not reflect a normal month, so re-check it
quiz.explanation: Saying what the data covers, and when to check again, lets the reader act sensibly on the result.
quiz.why_wrong: Hiding a limit misleads; festive weeks aren’t typical of the rest of the year; withholding the results helps no one.
quiz.learning_outcome: State the limits of your data and how to address them.

quiz.title: Did the loyalty programme pay?
quiz.scenario: The CFO asks whether the new loyalty programme paid for itself.
quiz.question: Which answer is most useful?
options: “Yes: engagement is up across app opens, reviews and referrals since the launch.”
“Yes: against a matched group, members spent ₹38 lakh more, costs were ₹22 lakh: ₹16 lakh net.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than non-members over six months, so it has clearly paid off.”
“It’s too early to say; loyalty programmes usually take a year to show results.”
quiz.explanation: It answers yes or no, in money, against a fair comparison, and says how the comparison was made.
quiz.why_wrong: Engagement doesn’t answer a money question; comparing members with all non-members ignores that loyal customers already spent more, and leaves out the cost; six months of data can already answer it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Answer the question asked, in its own terms.

questions.question: A manager asks, “Is our marketing working?” Which version of the question can an analysis actually answer?
options: “Are our Instagram and Google campaigns working, judging by the likes, clicks and reach they got in Q2?”
“What are all our marketing numbers for the last year, by channel and by month?”
“Did Q2 Instagram customers cost less per first order than Google ones, and should budget move?”
“Do customers like our ads, and which of them do they remember best?”
questions.explanation: It names the channels, the period, the measure and the decision it informs.

questions.question: Which of these is a category, not a quantity?
options: Payment method
Order value
Delivery minutes
Quantity ordered
questions.explanation: Payment method (UPI, card, cash on delivery) is a label; the others are amounts you can add or average.

questions.question: Which formula totals the order value for Pune from an Excel table called Orders?
options: =SUMIF(Orders[City], Orders[Value], "Pune")
=COUNTIFS(Orders[City], "Pune", Orders[Value], ">0")
=VLOOKUP("Pune", Orders[[City]:[Value]], 2, FALSE)
=SUMIFS(Orders[Value], Orders[City], "Pune")
questions.explanation: SUMIFS adds the values in one column where another column matches a condition.
questions.why_wrong: SUMIF takes the range to check, then the condition, then the values to add, so these arguments are in the wrong order; COUNTIFS counts Pune orders instead of adding their value; VLOOKUP returns only the first Pune order.

questions.question: Which pair of rows is a true duplicate that should be removed?
options: Two orders from the same customer, for the same product, on the same day
Two rows with the same order ID and identical values in every column
Two customers with the same name, living in the same city
Two rows with the same order value, date and payment method
questions.explanation: Only identical records with the same ID are duplicates; the others can be genuinely different records.

questions.question: 30% of survey respondents left their income blank. What is the best practice when reporting average income?
options: Fill the blanks with 0, so that every respondent is included in the average satisfaction score
Fill each blank with the average of those who answered, so the sample size isn’t reduced
Report the average for those who answered, the share missing, and whether skippers differ
Report the average of those who answered, without mentioning the blanks
questions.explanation: Being clear about who is included, and checking for a pattern in who skipped, keeps the result honest.

questions.question: What does this return? SELECT method, COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE amount > 1000 GROUP BY method;
options: The number of payments above ₹1,000 for each method
The total amount paid above ₹1,000, for each payment method
The payment methods that have more than 1,000 payments
The average payment for each method, for payments over ₹1,000
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps payments above ₹1,000; GROUP BY method with COUNT(*) counts them per method.

questions.question: What does an INNER JOIN between customers and orders return?
options: Every customer, with blank order columns for those without orders
Only customers without orders, with the order columns left blank
Every possible pair of a customer and an order, matched or not
Only customers who have orders, repeated once for each order
questions.explanation: An inner join keeps only rows that match in both tables, repeating a customer once per order.

questions.question: In a monthly revenue table, what does LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) give on each row?
options: Next month’s revenue, for comparing each month with the one after it
The previous month’s revenue, for working out month-on-month change
The running total of revenue from the first month up to that row
The lowest revenue in any earlier month, for spotting the worst month
questions.explanation: LAG looks back one row in the given order; LEAD would look forward.

questions.question: Median household spending is ₹18,000 and the mean is ₹31,000. What does this suggest?
options: Spending is spread evenly, and most households spend about ₹31,000
The data must contain errors, since the median and mean should be close
A few very high spenders pull the mean up: the data is skewed to the right
Most households spend more than ₹31,000, and a few spend very little
questions.explanation: When the mean is far above the median, a small number of large values is pulling it up.

questions.question: In an A/B test, version A converts 4.0% of 50,000 visitors and version B 4.1% of 50,000. Before calling B the winner, you should:
options: Check the gap is bigger than random variation, and that the test ran its planned length
Declare B the winner, since 50,000 visitors per version is plenty of data for a clear result
Run the test again in a single city, to see whether B wins there too
Add a third version, C, to see whether the gap between them grows
questions.explanation: A 0.1-point gap can easily be chance even with 50,000 visitors each; a significance check and the planned run length guard against a false winner.

questions.question: df.shape returns (48210, 12). What does that mean?
options: 48,210 columns and 12 rows
48,210 missing values
12 duplicate rows
48,210 rows and 12 columns

questions.question: After df = orders.merge(items, on="order_id"), the row count rises from 10,000 to 26,000. Why?
options: pandas added a blank row for every item with no matching order
Each order matches several items, so each order repeats once per item
The merge kept orders from both tables, including ones only in items
Some order IDs were read as text and others as numbers, so they doubled
questions.explanation: Joining one order to many items gives one row per item; summing order totals now would overcount.

questions.question: You are comparing the market share of 9 brands. Which chart is clearest?
options: A pie chart with 9 labelled slices
A line chart of share by brand
A sorted horizontal bar chart
A 3D pie chart with a legend
questions.explanation: Sorted bars make it easy to compare many categories and read their order; nine pie slices are hard to compare.

questions.question: An AI assistant says, “Your churn rate is 12%,” without showing how it worked it out. What should you do?
options: Ask how it was calculated (definition, period, data), reproduce it, then use it
Use it, since AI tools calculate rates more reliably than spreadsheets do
Ask the assistant to confirm it, and use it if it gives the same number again
Round it down to 10% to be safe, and note that it came from AI
questions.explanation: A number without a method can’t be trusted or explained; reproducing it confirms both.

questions.question: A one-page memo to a manager should open with:
options: The method you used, so readers trust what follows
A list of the data sources and the period covered
The background to the question and why it was asked
The recommendation and the key number behind it
questions.explanation: Busy readers decide from the first lines; method and sources belong further down.

project.brief: Analyse 12 months of data for a real or realistic Indian business (for example a D2C brand, a café chain, a clinic or a coaching centre) and recommend one change that would grow revenue or cut costs. Your mentor helps you choose the business, the question and a dataset (a public dataset, or anonymised data a business shares with you).
deliverables: A one-page problem statement: the decision, who makes it, and how success will be measured
The cleaned dataset, with a short data dictionary and a cleaning log
Your SQL queries or Python notebook, with comments explaining each step
A one-page dashboard (Power BI, Excel or Looker Studio) built around the decision
A one-page recommendation memo, and a 3-minute recorded walkthrough

rubric.name: Analysis
